questions.question: Define a Geographical Information System, name its five components, and explain why data is regarded as the most important and most expensive component.
questions.expected_answer: A GIS is a computerised system that captures, stores, analyses, manages and displays geographically referenced information — information tied to specific positions on the earth's surface, usually through coordinates. Its five components are hardware, the computers, servers, screens and GPS capture equipment; software, the programs such as QGIS or ArcGIS that store, analyse and display the layers; data, the georeferenced information itself; people, the trained operators, analysts and decision-makers; and procedures, the rules for checking, updating and verifying the data. Data is the most important and most expensive component because it is the system's model of reality: collecting and continually updating roads, clinics, settlements and census records costs more than any hardware, and if the data is outdated or wrong, the best hardware and software will still produce convincing but misleading results — an overlay analysis run on a five-year-old clinic layer can recommend building a clinic where one already exists. Procedures exist precisely to keep the data component reliable.

questions.question: Explain the layer principle and overlay analysis in a GIS, distinguishing between spatial and attribute data, and give an example of a planning question overlay analysis can answer.
questions.expected_answer: A GIS stores each theme of information about an area as a separate georeferenced layer — rivers on one, roads on another, settlements, rainfall and population density on others — all tied to the same coordinate system so any combination can be stacked in perfect alignment over the same ground, like transparent sheets held to the light. Overlay analysis is the combining of layers to answer questions no single map could: for example, stacking population density, existing clinics and roads to find densely populated places more than ten kilometres from any clinic but close to a road, which is where a new clinic should go; or overlaying schools on a floodplain layer to find schools at risk. For every feature, the GIS stores spatial data — where the feature is and its shape — and attribute data — the descriptive facts about it, such as a school's name, learner numbers and language of instruction. Selecting a feature on the map opens its attribute table, and this link between position and description is the heart of the system.

questions.question: Define remote sensing, distinguish satellite images from aerial photographs, and discuss how remote sensing supports population studies in South Africa, including its main limitation.
questions.expected_answer: Remote sensing is the gathering of information about the earth's surface from a distance, without physical contact, using sensors on satellites or aircraft that measure reflected energy, including wavelengths invisible to the eye such as infrared. Satellite images, from platforms such as Landsat — recording since 1972 — and Sentinel, cover enormous areas at coarser detail and revisit the same ground on a fixed cycle, building a time series ideal for detecting change such as urban growth, drought and dam levels. Aerial photographs are taken from far lower altitudes, showing fine detail over small areas; corrected orthophotos form the base of South Africa's 1 to 10 000 orthophoto maps. For population work, satellite images taken months apart reveal new roof clusters on the informal edges of cities like Johannesburg, eThekwini and Cape Town, which become GIS layers overlaid with water, sanitation and clinic layers to direct services; Statistics South Africa uses imagery to delimit census enumeration areas so no dwelling is missed; and after the April 2022 KwaZulu-Natal floods, before-and-after images located destroyed neighbourhoods and cut roads while the ground was impassable. SANSA receives satellite data at Hartebeesthoek. The main limitation is that sensors register structures, not lives: remote sensing counts roofs but cannot record who lives beneath them, their ages, languages or incomes, so the ground census remains irreplaceable.
